newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Focus on 6.50-pct long bond.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Focus on 6.50-pct long bond.

text.p: U.S. Treasury market players will focus on Thursday on whether the 30-year bond can hold to the impressive gains scored on the latest news about the tame U.S. inflation, analysts said.
The 30-year lond bond yield closed below the key 6.50-percent level on Wednesday for the first time since December, 1996.
"The (Treasury) market is going to see if it can hold on to these gains," predicted Kim Rupert, senior economist at MMS International.
U.S. Treasuries ended sharply higher on Wednesday with the benchmark 30-year bond closing up 28/32 at 101-29/32 to yield 6.48 percent.
Traders said breaking through the 6.50-percent psychological barrier was a bullish sign but needed confirmation.

Commenting on the U.S. data coming out on Thursday, Rupert said the "housing starts might be important but people are already expecting a fairly decent rebound. Nevertheless, given where the market, is we could see some profit-taking on strong numbers."

Carey Leahey, chief U.S. economist at High Frequency Economics, said bond market participants would prefer to focus on the Federal Reserve Bank of Philiadelphia's July survey of regional business activity.
"It is not a particularly reliable indicator of the manufacturing sector -- but it is the freshest game in town," said Leahey.

"We'll be talking about late June and early July figures and the bond market loves timely information, even if it's not of high quality, so the 10 o'clock (1600 GMT) number will be the big number," Leahy added.
Analysts forecast the Philadelphia Fed's July index will come out at a reading of 18 versus 25.2 in the prior report.

"The market is aware of the fact that the manufacturing sector is still pretty healthy ... we did see a huge jump in June though, but most people think the number will come down off of that," said MMS International's Rupert who expected a decline to about 19.
The consensus forecast for the June U.S. housing starts -- due out at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT -- is for a rise to an annualized rate of 1.45 million units versus 1.397 million in the prior month.

"While we've gotton a whole ton of good news this week on the (U.S.) economy, particulary inflation, the market might get upset tomorrow when it sees a pretty hefty bounceback in housing starts," cautioned Mickey Levy, chief financial economist at Nationsbanc Capital Markets Inc.

But High Frequency's Leahey made the opposite argument that, "if there were to see a big drop (in housing starts), the market would scream ... we've broken through a big technical resistance of 6.50 percent on the long bond."
Also, on tap for Thursday is the Labor Department's release of weekly U.S. initial claims for unemployment.
In a Reuters poll, economists predict a drop to 345,000 in the jobless claims for the week ended July 12 from 377,000 in the prior week.
"There's kind of a tricky period right now with auto retooling and seasonal factors ... Most people think they'll come off the sharp increase from last week," cautioned Rupert at MMS.
Meanwhile, Leahy agreed "claims will be of some interest ... mainly if they remain well above 350,000. That could be bullish for the market as it would indicate the economy is really softening."
